#!/usr/bin/env bash
# core/pipeline/strategies/map.sh — data-driven map over any declared list dimension (issue #1285)
# ADR-047: generalizes fanout (platforms) to arbitrary declared dimensions.
# When dimension=platforms, behavior is byte-identical to _strategy_run_fanout.
# Sourced library: inherits caller's pipefail; do not add set -euo pipefail here.

[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_STRATEGY_MAP_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
_ZBUILD_STRATEGY_MAP_LOADED=1

_ZBUILD_STRATEGIES_DIR_MAP="$(cd "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}" 2>/dev/null || true; pwd)"
source "${_ZBUILD_STRATEGIES_DIR_MAP}/common.sh"

# ─── _strategy_map_resolve_dimension ─────────────────────────────────────────
# Resolves the iteration list for the given dimension name.
# For "platforms": uses _DETECTED_PLATFORMS (set by runner before dispatch).
# For other names: uses _MAP_DIM_<name> array if set; otherwise empty.
# Prints one element per line; no output = empty dimension.
_strategy_map_resolve_dimension() {
    local dim="${1:-platforms}"
    if [[ "$dim" == "platforms" ]]; then
        local p
        for p in "${_DETECTED_PLATFORMS[@]+"${_DETECTED_PLATFORMS[@]}"}"; do
            [[ -n "$p" ]] && printf '%s\n' "$p"
        done
        return 0
    fi
    # Arbitrary dimension: caller must export _MAP_DIM_<name> as an array.
    # Validate dimension name to prevent variable-name injection.
    if [[ ! "$dim" =~ ^[a-zA-Z0-9_]{1,64}$ ]]; then
        warn "map: invalid dimension name: ${dim}" || true
        return 1
    fi
    # Read the caller's _MAP_DIM_<name> array by reference (Bash 5+ floor — see
    # scripts/lib/compat.sh). The name was validated above, guarding the target.
    # The array lives in the caller's scope (same sourced shell). Guarded
    # expansion tolerates an unset target under the caller's `set -u`.
    local -n _ref="_MAP_DIM_${dim}"
    local elem
    for elem in "${_ref[@]+"${_ref[@]}"}"; do
        [[ -n "$elem" ]] && printf '%s\n' "$elem"
    done
}

# ─── _strategy_map_resolve_max ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# Resolves the max_parallel concurrency cap for a map group.
# Input: raw max value from template (_TPL_MAP_MAX_<gid>), e.g. "4", "auto", "".
# Mirrors _parallel_resolve_max (parallel-orchestrator.sh) EXACTLY so map and
# parallel groups agree on the cap and its fail-safe:
#   - explicit positive integer  → used as-is (then capped at _PARALLEL_MAX_JOBS_CAP)
#   - "auto" / empty             → ZBUILD_PARALLEL_JOBS env override, else CPU count
#   - ANYTHING else (non-numeric typo, "0", negative) → CLAMPED TO 1 (fail-safe).
# #1312 (Copilot): an invalid template value must NOT silently remove the cap by
# falling through to CPU-count concurrency — that is the opposite of safe. Clamp to 1.
_strategy_map_resolve_max() {
    local raw="${1:-}"
    # #1312 (Copilot): reuse the parallel path's readonly cap so map and parallel
    # stay in sync if it ever changes — don't duplicate the literal. Falls back to 8
    # only when map.sh is sourced standalone (unit tests) without the parallel module.
    local cap="${_PARALLEL_MAX_JOBS_CAP:-8}"
    local max="$raw"
    # "auto" is an explicit request for the CPU-based default (map-specific alias);
    # normalise it to empty so the empty-branch resolves the default.
    [[ "$max" == "auto" ]] && max=""
    if [[ -z "$max" ]]; then
        if [[ "${ZBUILD_PARALLEL_JOBS:-}" =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]]; then
            max="$ZBUILD_PARALLEL_JOBS"
        else
            max="$( { nproc 2>/dev/null || sysctl -n hw.ncpu 2>/dev/null; } | head -1 )"  # sigpipe-ok: writer emits exactly one line

        fi
    fi

    [[ "$max" =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || max=1

}

#   strategy.unit_name_conflict event says why. Not subject to on_member_error.
# _map_unit_element <var> <role_count> <role> <element> — sets <var> to the part
# of a member's unit name after the stage (#1706): the element, or
# <role>.<element> when the map runs more than one role. No subshell per member.
_map_unit_element() {
    if [[ "$2" -gt 1 ]]; then printf -v "$1" '%s.%s' "$3" "$4"; else printf -v "$1" '%s' "$4"; fi
}

# _map_write_summary <stage> <state_file> <env_target> <n> <plugin_dir…> <element…>
# #2368: the engine sums up a map group — every element, its outcome and its
# one-line reason, read from the element's own primary result — into
# artifacts/<stage>-summary.md, and tells later stages whether any element
# failed (ZBUILD_RUN_FLAGGED=yes|no). Fail-open: a diagnostic never fails the group.
_map_write_summary() {
    local stage="$1" state_file="$2" env_target="$3" n="$4"; shift 4
    local -a plugins=("${@:1:$n}") elems=("${@:$((n + 1)):$n}")
    local state_dir art i raw res line body="" flagged=no outcome reason
    state_dir="$(dirname "$state_file")"; art="${ZBUILD_ARTIFACT_DIR:-$state_dir/artifacts}"
    declare -F _registry_output_path_rows >/dev/null 2>&1 \
        || source "$(cd "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}" 2>/dev/null || true; cd "../../plugin-registry" && pwd)/output-paths.sh" 2>/dev/null || true
    for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )); do
        raw="$(_registry_output_path_rows "${plugins[$i]}/manifest.yaml" 2>/dev/null | awk -F'\t' '$2=="true"{print $1; exit}')"
        res=""
        if [[ -n "$raw" ]]; then
            if [[ -n "$env_target" ]]; then
                res="$(export "$env_target=${elems[$i]}"; _registry_resolve_output_path "$raw" "$state_dir" "$art")"
            else
                _registry_resolve_output_path_v res "$raw" "$state_dir" "$art"
            fi
        fi
        outcome="missing"; reason=""
        if [[ -n "$res" && -s "$res" ]]; then
            outcome="$(jq -r '.outcome // "missing"' "$res" 2>/dev/null || echo missing)"
            reason="$(jq -r '(.reason // "") | gsub("[\r\n]+"; " ")' "$res" 2>/dev/null || true)"
        fi
        [[ "$outcome" == fail ]] && flagged=yes
        line="- ${elems[$i]}: $outcome${reason:+ — $reason}"
        body+="$line"$'\n'
    done
    export ZBUILD_RUN_FLAGGED="$flagged"
    mkdir -p "$art" 2>/dev/null || true
    printf '## %s\n\n%s' "$stage" "$body" > "$art/${stage//[^A-Za-z0-9_.-]/_}-summary.md" 2>/dev/null || true
    return 0
}

_strategy_run_map() {
    # #1850 (ADR-054 §4): rc is 0 or 1; WHY rides this word, which the caller
    # reads in the same shell — ok | partial | empty | no_plugin | bad_dimension
    # | infra_failed | failed.
    _ZB_STRATEGY_OUTCOME="failed"
    local pool_id="$1" stage="$2" roles_out="$3" state_file="$4" plugins_root="$5"
    local dimension="${6:-platforms}" env_target="${7:-}"
    local max_raw="${8:-}" on_member_error="${9:-collect}"
    local success_count=0 fail_count=0 any_plugin_found=false

    # Resolve the iteration list. Capture output AND rc explicitly — a process
    # substitution would discard the resolver's status, collapsing an invalid
    # dimension (rc=2) into the empty path (rc=3) and masking a fail-closed error.
    local _resolved _res_rc
    _resolved="$(_strategy_map_resolve_dimension "$dimension")"; _res_rc=$?
    if [[ $_res_rc -ne 0 ]]; then
        # Invalid/unknown dimension name — fail closed. Distinct from empty (rc=3);
        # the runner does NOT map rc=5 to 0, so this surfaces as a real failure.
        orch_shutdown "$pool_id" 2>/dev/null || true
        _ZB_STRATEGY_OUTCOME="bad_dimension"
        return 1
    fi

    local -a elements=()
    local _elem
    while IFS= read -r _elem; do
        [[ -n "$_elem" ]] && elements+=("$_elem")
    done <<< "$_resolved"

    if [[ ${#elements[@]} -eq 0 ]]; then
        orch_shutdown "$pool_id" 2>/dev/null || true
        _ZB_STRATEGY_OUTCOME="empty"
        return 0
    fi

    # #1312: resolve the concurrency cap (mirrors ADR-039 FIFO pool).
    local max_parallel
    max_parallel="$(_strategy_map_resolve_max "$max_raw")"

    # #1706 (ADR-054 §3.1): every member runs under <stage>.<element>. Two
    # members with one name would write the same records at the same time, so
    # the group is refused before any member starts.
    # With more than one role every role runs on every element, so the role is
    # part of the name: <stage>.<role>.<element>.
    local -A _unit_seen=()
    local _u_role _u_elem _u_name _u_roles=0
    while IFS= read -r _u_role; do [[ -n "$_u_role" ]] && _u_roles=$((_u_roles + 1)); done <<< "$roles_out"
    while IFS= read -r _u_role; do
        [[ -z "$_u_role" ]] && continue
        for _u_elem in "${elements[@]}"; do
            _map_unit_element _u_name "$_u_roles" "$_u_role" "$_u_elem"; _u_name="${stage}.${_u_name}"
            if [[ -n "${_unit_seen[$_u_name]:-}" ]]; then
                warn "map: two members of '$stage' would both run as '$_u_name' — refusing the group" || true

                orch_shutdown "$pool_id" 2>/dev/null || true
                return 1
            fi
            _unit_seen[$_u_name]=1
        done
    done <<< "$roles_out"

    # Build the ordered list of (plugin_dir, element) work items by iterating
    # roles × elements — same order as before, just collected before dispatch.
    local -a wu_list=() plugin_list=() elem_list=()
    local role element plugin_dir wu
    while IFS= read -r role; do
        [[ -z "$role" ]] && continue
        for element in "${elements[@]}"; do
            # Mirror fanout.sh platform-specific then generic resolution.
            plugin_dir="$(resolve_plugin_for_role "$role" "$element" "$plugins_root" 2>/dev/null || true)"
            [[ -z "$plugin_dir" ]] && \
                plugin_dir="$(resolve_plugin_for_role "$role" "" "$plugins_root" 2>/dev/null || true)"
            [[ -z "$plugin_dir" ]] && continue
            any_plugin_found=true

            # Only the platforms dimension populates ZBUILD_PLATFORM (ADR-009 §6
            # env contract) — pass the element as the 4th arg so the platforms
            # path stays byte-identical to fanout. For non-platform dimensions
            # (lenses/mutants), pass the generic element identity via args 5+6
            # (ZBUILD_MAP_ELEMENT / ZBUILD_MAP_DIMENSION, issue #1295, ADR-047 §2)
            # so each work unit is distinguishable without hijacking ZBUILD_PLATFORM.
            # An optional env_target (arg 7, from the template's `as:`) additionally
            # sets a named env var to the element — a generic mapping the strategy
            # applies without knowing which dimension or var it is.
            _map_unit_element _u_elem "$_u_roles" "$role" "$element"

# ── ADR-054 §7 (#1829) / #1831: always-run stages on EVERY exit path ─────
    # Success, non-zero rc, SIGINT, SIGTERM and timeout all funnel through the
    # EXIT trap below, which is why the dispatch lives there and not at the end
    # of main() — an exit path that skipped it would leak whatever the stage
    # spawned. #1759 is the prerequisite: without re-armed INT/TERM traps there
    # is no signal path for this to hang off.
    #
    # #1831: WHICH stages run here is the TEMPLATE's decision, not the engine's.
    # This used to name one plugin by directory (`plugins/tool/teardown`) and
    # degrade to a no-op if it was absent — the engine knowing one plugin's path
    # is the coupling ADR-047 forbids, and a silent no-op is how #1878's sibling
    # mechanism went uninvoked without anything noticing. The list now comes
    # from the template's `always_run:`, resolved by role through the same
    # `resolve_plugin_for_role` seam every dispatch strategy uses.
    #
    # Scope stays pinned to `release` for the teardown role: free live resources
    # and delete NOTHING, so a failed run keeps all of its evidence on disk.
    # `purge` is operator-only and unreachable from any run path.
    _runner_dispatch_always_run() {
        [[ -n "${_runner_state_file:-}" && -f "${_runner_state_file}" ]] || return 0
        [[ "${#_TPL_ALWAYS_RUN[@]}" -gt 0 ]] || return 0
        local plugins_root="${ZBUILD_PLUGINS_ROOT:-$_ZBUILD_ROOT/plugins}"
        local _ar_stage _ar_safe _ar_role _ar_to _ar_dir _ar_guard
        for _ar_stage in "${_TPL_ALWAYS_RUN[@]}"; do
            _ar_safe="${_ar_stage//-/_}"
            # Per-stage, not global: the trap can be reached more than once, and
            # there is now more than one always-run stage to keep track of.
            _ar_guard="_RUNNER_AR_DISPATCHED_${_ar_safe}"
            [[ "${!_ar_guard:-0}" == "1" ]] && continue
            printf -v "$_ar_guard" '%s' 1

            local _ar_roles_var="_TPL_STAGE_ROLES_${_ar_safe}"
            _ar_role="${!_ar_roles_var:-}"
            [[ -n "$_ar_role" ]] || continue
            # roles: is a list; an always-run stage takes the first.
            _ar_role="${_ar_role%%,*}"

            _ar_dir="$(resolve_plugin_for_role "$_ar_role" "" "$plugins_root" 2>/dev/null || true)"
            if [[ -z "$_ar_dir" || ! -d "$_ar_dir" ]]; then
                # LOUD, unlike the old `[[ -d ... ]] || return 0`. An always-run
                # stage that cannot be resolved has not run, and the operator
                # needs to know that rather than infer it from a missing effect.
                eb_emit_event "stage.always_run.unresolved" "stage=$_ar_stage" "role=$_ar_role" 2>/dev/null || true
                continue
            fi

            _ar_to="$(template_stage_time_limit "$_ar_stage")"

            # Bounded, because this runs inside the EXIT trap: a hook that blocks
            # would turn a Ctrl-C into a hang — the exact class of bug this
            # mechanism exists to prevent. A timeout BINARY cannot be used here
            # (plugin_hook_call is a shell function; timeout can only exec a
            # command, so the wrapper would fail with "command not found" and
            # silently skip every dispatch). The bound is therefore a watchdog
            # that is CANCELLED on the normal path, so no stray `sleep` outlives
            # the run.
            #
            # `|| true` because an always-run stage's failure is recorded as an
            # event and must NEVER change the run's exit status.
            #
            # #2287: the bound must stop the hook, not just stop waiting for it.
            # Signalling the one PID reached only the outer shell: the subshell
            # running the stage hooks, and anything it spawned, lived on after
            # the run and wrote into its state minutes later. `set -m` (as the
            # router's model spawn does, #2056) makes each job a process-group
            # leader, so zbuild_pg_kill reaches the whole tree — TERM then KILL
            # after a grace for a hook that traps TERM. The watchdog gets its own
            # group too, so cancelling it leaves no `sleep` behind. (#1801)
            (
                export ZBUILD_TEARDOWN_SCOPE=release
                set -m
                plugin_hook_call "$_ar_dir" run "$_ar_stage" "$_runner_state_file" &
                _ar_pid=$!
                ( set +m; sleep "$_ar_to"; zbuild_pg_kill "$_ar_pid" ) &
                _wd_pid=$!
                set +m
                # A signal to the run's group (`timeout` sends its TERM there a
                # second time) must not end this wait, or the KILL below would
                # stop the stage before its bound.
                trap ':' INT TERM  # waits out a repeat signal (above)
                while kill -0 "$_ar_pid" 2>/dev/null; do wait "$_ar_pid" 2>/dev/null || true; done
                # #2333: the leader exiting does not mean its group did. A member
                # that ignored TERM would lose its KILL when the watchdog is
                # cancelled below, so kill the group now; a no-op when it is gone.
                zbuild_pg_kill "$_ar_pid"
                kill -TERM -- -"$_wd_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
                wait "$_wd_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
            ) >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
        done
        return 0
    }

    _runner_abort_trap() {
        _runner_restore_stderr
        # ADR-054 §7: a signal ends the run while a stage is still running;
        # stop it, and all it started, before anything else.
        declare -F plugin_stop_running >/dev/null 2>&1 && plugin_stop_running
        # #1829: free live resources first, while the state file and the
        # process tree are still intact.
        _runner_dispatch_always_run
        # #1688: release the issue lock EXPLICITLY. Relying on process death is
        # not enough — a flock belongs to the open file description, which every
        # child inherits, so one lingering child would keep the issue locked
        # after this run is gone. Released after the always-run stages, which
        # still belong to this run.
        if declare -F zbuild_issue_lock_release >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            zbuild_issue_lock_release || true
        fi
        if declare -F zbuild_run_cap_release >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            zbuild_run_cap_release || true
        fi
        # ADR-025 (Wave 15-B #684): the sentinel must be cleared on EVERY
        # exit path — clean end, normal failure, or abort — so a follow-on
        # zbuild invocation in the same state_dir never sees a stale
        # signal. Runs BEFORE the short-circuit because the
        # `_runner_ended=true` path is the common case (every successful
        # run hits it) and that path also needs the cleanup.
        _zbuild_disarm_abort_sentinel
        # Best-effort: drop THIS run's own lock siblings so a killed run does
        # not leave a stale .lock behind. flock releases on fd close at process

68	# during startup, long before any stage is dispatched, so waiting on it and then
69	# sleeping a second is not "the stage has started" — it is a guess that happens to
70	# hold on an idle machine.
71	#
72	# On a loaded one it does not, and SPEC-4 then SIGTERMs a runner still setting up
73	# its worktree: no stage has run, no release hook is armed, no marker is written,
74	# and the assertion reports a missing file with no hint that the run never got
75	# that far. Observed directly — `wait` returned in 0s, the hook-entered marker was
76	# absent, and the runner's last line was "Working in the run's worktree".
77	#
78	# `runner-release-exit-paths-test.sh` already does this correctly with
79	# BUILD_STARTED; this is the same idea. The marker can only appear once the stage
80	# is genuinely executing, so load can only delay it, never fake it.
81	# #1850: the stage writes the v2 result its manifest (mock_plugin_factory's)
82	# promises — pass on rc 0, error/broken otherwise — so a run that should succeed
83	# is not failed for leaving no readable result.
84	_arm_outcome() {
85	    local _o=pass
86	    [[ "${2:-0}" -ne 0 ]] && _o=broken
87	    cat > "$PLUGINS_ROOT/agent/outcome/plugin.sh" <<PLUG
88	outcome_run() {
89	    : > "\${STAGE_STARTED:-/dev/null}"
90	    ${1:-:}
91	    $(mock_result_line outcome "$_o")
92	    return ${2:-0}
93	}
94	PLUG
95	}
96	
97	# Each case gets its own state dir: a stale marker or state file from a prior
98	# case would make a later one pass for the wrong reason.
99	_run_case() {
100	    local name="$1" rc_want_set="$2"
101	    rm -f "$RELEASE_MARKER" "$RELEASE_ENTERED"
102	    export ZBUILD_STATE_DIR="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/state-$name"
103	    mkdir -p "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR"
104	    set +e
105	    ( cd "$OVERLAY_REPO" && bash "$RUNNER" --template always-run-minimal \
106	        --goal "always-run $name" ) >"$TEST_TEMP_DIR/$name.out" 2>&1
107	    _CASE_RC=$?
108	    set -e
109	    [[ "$rc_want_set" == "skip" ]] || true
110	}
111	
112	# ─── [SPEC-1][change] rc=0 — the ordinary success path ──────────────────────
113	print_test_section "[SPEC-1][change] release runs when the pipeline succeeds"
114	_arm_release; _arm_outcome "" 0
115	_run_case "rc0" skip
116	assert_file_exists "[SPEC-1] release ran on rc=0" "$RELEASE_MARKER"
117	
118	# ─── [SPEC-2][change] rc=1 — a failed run still frees its resources ─────────
119	# The failing path is the one that matters most: a run that died is exactly the
120	# run holding process groups and locks nobody else will clean up.
121	print_test_section "[SPEC-2][change] release runs when a stage fails"
122	_arm_release; _arm_outcome "" 1
123	_run_case "rc1" skip
124	assert_file_exists "[SPEC-2] release ran on a non-zero stage rc" "$RELEASE_MARKER"
125	
126	# ─── [SPEC-3][change] the SIGINT path ─────────────────────────────────────
127	# #1850 (ADR-054 §4, ADR-025): the SIGINT path is the recorded abort word, not
128	# rc=130 — a bare 130 from a stage is just a failed stage now. So the stage
129	# does what a Ctrl-C does to the process group: the sentinel is armed (empty =
130	# sigint) and the child dies with 130. The run must end on the abort path —
131	# exit 1, status interrupted — or this case would only repeat SPEC-2.
132	print_test_section "[SPEC-3][change] release runs on the SIGINT path (abort word sigint)"
133	_arm_release
134	# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # expanded by the stage at run time, not here
135	_arm_outcome ': > "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR/.abort.signal"' 130
136	_run_case "rc130" skip
137	assert_file_exists "[SPEC-3] release ran on the SIGINT path" "$RELEASE_MARKER"
138	assert_eq "[SPEC-3] the run took the abort path: exit 1 (not 130), status interrupted" \
139	    "1 interrupted" "$_CASE_RC $(jq -r '.status // "MISSING"' "$TEST_TEMP_DIR/state-rc130/pipeline-state.json" 2>/dev/null)"
140	
141	# ─── [SPEC-4][change] SIGTERM delivered to the runner itself ───────────────
142	# Distinct from SPEC-3: there the stage returned a code, here the signal is
143	# delivered to the runner process while a stage is still executing. #1759's
144	# re-armed INT/TERM traps are what give this path somewhere to hang off.
145	print_test_section "[SPEC-4][change] release runs when the runner is SIGTERMed mid-stage"
146	_arm_release; _arm_outcome "sleep 30" 0
147	rm -f "$RELEASE_MARKER" "$RELEASE_ENTERED"
148	export ZBUILD_STATE_DIR="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/state-sigterm"
149	export STAGE_STARTED="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/stage-started-sigterm"
150	rm -f "$STAGE_STARTED"
151	mkdir -p "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR"
152	( cd "$OVERLAY_REPO" && bash "$RUNNER" --template always-run-minimal \
153	    --goal "always-run sigterm" ) >"$TEST_TEMP_DIR/sigterm.out" 2>&1 &
154	_runner_pid=$!
155	# Wait for the run to actually reach the stage before signalling — signalling a
156	# runner still in startup would prove nothing about the exit path.
157	#
158	# #2029: this used to wait for `pipeline-state.json` and then sleep 1. That file
159	# is written during STARTUP, so the wait proved nothing and the sleep was the only
160	# real margin. Under load it was not enough and the signal landed mid-startup.
161	# STAGE_STARTED is written by the stage itself, so it cannot be reached early.
162	_waited=0
163	while [[ ! -f "$STAGE_STARTED" && $_waited -lt 300 ]]; do
164	    sleep 0.2; _waited=$(( _waited + 1 ))
165	done
166	if [[ ! -f "$STAGE_STARTED" ]]; then
167	    assert_fail "[SPEC-4] the stage started before the signal was sent" \
168	        "STAGE_STARTED never appeared in 60s — the run never reached a stage, so the exit path was never exercised"
169	fi
170	_spec4_t0=$(date +%s)
171	kill -TERM "$_runner_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
172	wait "$_runner_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
173	_spec4_wait_s=$(( $(date +%s) - _spec4_t0 ))
174	# The trap runs in the dying process; give it a moment to land the marker.
175	_waited=0
176	while [[ ! -f "$RELEASE_MARKER" && $_waited -lt 50 ]]; do
177	    sleep 0.2; _waited=$(( _waited + 1 ))
178	done
179	
180	# #2029: say WHAT WAS SEEN, not merely that the file is absent.
181	#
182	# This assertion has failed intermittently on CI for as long as it has existed,
183	# and it could never be diagnosed because "file not found" is the same output
184	# whether the runner ignored the signal, died before its trap, ran teardown into
185	# a different path, or simply had not finished yet. Three separate mechanisms
186	# were proposed for it and all three were disproven.
187	#
188	# The sibling assertion in runner-release-exit-paths prints the marker it read,
189	# and that one line is what let #2046 identify its cause in minutes after days of
190	# guessing. This is that lesson applied here: the next occurrence explains itself
191	# instead of starting another hunt.
192	if [[ ! -f "$RELEASE_MARKER" ]]; then
193	    {
194	        printf '  DIAGNOSTIC [SPEC-4]: release marker absent after %ss of polling\n' "$(( _waited * 2 / 10 ))"
195	        printf '    wait on the runner returned after: %ss\n' "$_spec4_wait_s"
196	        printf '    runner pid %s still alive: %s\n' "$_runner_pid" \
197	            "$(kill -0 "$_runner_pid" 2>/dev/null && echo YES || echo no)"
198	        printf '    release hook ENTERED marker: %s\n' \
199	            "$([[ -f "$RELEASE_ENTERED" ]] && echo present || echo absent)"
200	        printf '    state dir: %s\n' \
201	            "$([[ -d "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR" ]] && (cd "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR" && printf '%s ' * 2>/dev/null) || echo '<missing>')"
202	        printf '    runner output (last 5 lines):\n'
203	        tail -5 "$TEST_TEMP_DIR/sigterm.out" 2>/dev/null | sed 's/^/      /' || printf '      <no output>\n'
204	    } >&2
205	fi
206	# RELEASE_ENTERED separates "the hook never started" from "it started and did not
207	# finish" — the single most useful split, and the one the bare check cannot make.
208	assert_file_exists "[SPEC-4] release ran after SIGTERM to the runner" "$RELEASE_MARKER"
209	
210	# ─── [SPEC-5][guard] a hanging release cannot hang the exit ────────────────
211	# The stage declares timeout_s: 2. A hook that blocks past it must be killed and
212	# the exit must continue — otherwise Ctrl-C becomes a lockup, which is the exact
213	# class of bug an EXIT-trap dispatch exists to avoid. Asserting the WALL CLOCK
214	# rather than the marker: the marker would also be absent if release never ran
215	# at all, so it cannot distinguish "bounded" from "broken".
216	print_test_section "[SPEC-5][guard] a release hook that hangs is bounded by its timeout_s"
217	_arm_release "sleep 60"; _arm_outcome "" 0
218	rm -f "$RELEASE_MARKER" "$RELEASE_ENTERED"
219	export ZBUILD_STATE_DIR="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/state-hang"
220	mkdir -p "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR"
221	_t0=$(date +%s)
222	set +e
223	( cd "$OVERLAY_REPO" && bash "$RUNNER" --template always-run-minimal \
224	    --goal "always-run hang" ) >"$TEST_TEMP_DIR/hang.out" 2>&1
225	set -e
226	_elapsed=$(( $(date +%s) - _t0 ))
227	# 45s is generous against a 2s bound plus runner startup; the assertion is
228	# "bounded at all", not a tight budget — a tight one would flake under a loaded
229	# parallel pool (the #991 lesson).
230	if [[ "$_elapsed" -lt 45 ]]; then
231	    assert_pass "[SPEC-5] a 60s release hook did not hold the exit (${_elapsed}s)"
232	else
233	    assert_fail "[SPEC-5] a 60s release hook held the exit" "elapsed=${_elapsed}s"
234	fi
235	# These two together are what make the case meaningful: the hook WAS entered
236	# (so the bound is what stopped it) and did NOT complete (so it was actually
237	# killed). Either alone is satisfied by a dispatch that never happened.
238	assert_file_exists "[SPEC-5] the hanging hook was actually dispatched" "$RELEASE_ENTERED"
239	assert_file_not_exists "[SPEC-5] the hanging hook was killed before completing" "$RELEASE_MARKER"
240	
241	# ─── [#1801/SPEC-5]: persist always_run stage bounded by timeout_s: (not 120s) ─
242	# _runner_dispatch_always_run must use template_stage_time_limit (top-level
243	# timeout_s:) instead of ZBUILD_RELEASE_TIMEOUT / router.timeout_s.
244	# The fixture template sets persist.timeout_s: 4 (new code reads) and
245	# persist.router.timeout_s: 120 (old code reads ZBUILD_RELEASE_TIMEOUT / router.timeout_s).
246	# A blocking persist hook must be killed in ~4s, NOT ~120s.
247	# FAILS on old code (elapsed ~120s > 20), PASSES on new code (elapsed ~4s < 20).
248	print_test_section "[#1801/SPEC-5] persist always_run watchdog uses timeout_s: not router.timeout_s: 120"
249	mkdir -p "$PLUGINS_ROOT/tool/persist"
250	cat > "$PLUGINS_ROOT/tool/persist/manifest.yaml" <<'MF'
251	id: persist
252	name: Persist Stub Spec5
253	kind: tool
254	version: 0.0.1
255	hooks:
256	  run: persist_run
257	requires:
258	  core:
259	    - redaction
260	provides:
261	  role: persist
262	MF
263	_SPEC5P_ENTERED="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/spec5p-entered"
264	_SPEC5P_DONE="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/spec5p-done"
265	cat > "$PLUGINS_ROOT/tool/persist/plugin.sh" <<PLUG
266	persist_run() {
267	    : > "${_SPEC5P_ENTERED}"
268	    sleep 120
269	    : > "${_SPEC5P_DONE}"
270	    return 0
271	}
272	PLUG
273	
274	_spec5p_repo="$(setup_git_temp_repo "always-run-spec5p")"
275	install_template_overlay "$_spec5p_repo" always-run-minimal
276	if [[ -d "$_spec5p_repo/.git/info" ]] && \
277	   ! grep -qxF '/.zbuild/' "$_spec5p_repo/.git/info/exclude" 2>/dev/null; then
278	    printf '/.zbuild/\n' >> "$_spec5p_repo/.git/info/exclude"
279	fi
280	cat > "$_spec5p_repo/.zbuild/templates/always-run-spec5p.yaml" <<'YAML'
281	id: always-run-spec5p
282	extends: always-run-minimal
283	always_run:
284	  - release
285	  - persist
286	persist:
287	  gate: auto
288	  roles: [persist]
289	  timeout_s: 4
290	  router:
291	    timeout_s: 120
292	  io:
293	    destinations: [file]
294	    tail_lines: 50
295	YAML
296	_arm_outcome "" 0
297	_arm_release
298	rm -f "$_SPEC5P_ENTERED" "$_SPEC5P_DONE"
299	export ZBUILD_STATE_DIR="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/state-spec5p"
300	export ZBUILD_EVENTS_JSONL="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/events/spec5p-events.jsonl"
301	mkdir -p "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR"
302	_spec5p_t0=$(date +%s)
303	set +e
304	( cd "$_spec5p_repo" && bash "$RUNNER" --template always-run-spec5p \
305	    --goal "spec5-persist" ) >"$TEST_TEMP_DIR/spec5p.out" 2>&1
306	set -e
307	_spec5p_elapsed=$(( $(date +%s) - _spec5p_t0 ))
308	if [[ "$_spec5p_elapsed" -lt 20 ]]; then
309	    assert_pass "[#1801/SPEC-5] persist always_run watchdog bounds at timeout_s: 4 (exited in ${_spec5p_elapsed}s; old code: router.timeout_s: 120)"
310	else
311	    assert_fail "[#1801/SPEC-5] persist always_run watchdog must use timeout_s: 4" \
312	        "runner took ${_spec5p_elapsed}s; expected < 20s (timeout_s: 4); old code reads router.timeout_s: 120 → ~120s"
313	fi
314	assert_file_exists "[#1801/SPEC-5] persist hook was entered (always_run persist stage dispatched)" "$_SPEC5P_ENTERED"
315	assert_file_not_exists "[#1801/SPEC-5] persist hook killed before completing (bounded by timeout_s: 4, not 120s)" "$_SPEC5P_DONE"
316	
317	# ─── [SPEC-6][guard] an unresolvable always-run role is LOUD ───────────────
318	# The code this replaces did `[[ -d "$_td_dir" ]] || return 0` — a missing
319	# plugin was a silent no-op. An always-run stage that cannot be resolved has not
320	# run, and the operator must be able to see that rather than infer it from a
321	# missing effect.
322	print_test_section "[SPEC-6][guard] an unresolvable role emits an event instead of failing silently"
323	_arm_outcome "" 0
324	rm -f "$RELEASE_MARKER"
325	rm -rf "$PLUGINS_ROOT/tool/teardown"
326	export ZBUILD_STATE_DIR="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/state-unresolved"
327	export ZBUILD_EVENTS_JSONL="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/events/unresolved.jsonl"
328	mkdir -p "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR"
329	set +e
330	( cd "$OVERLAY_REPO" && bash "$RUNNER" --template always-run-minimal \
331	    --goal "always-run unresolved" ) >"$TEST_TEMP_DIR/unresolved.out" 2>&1
332	_unres_rc=$?
333	set -e
334	assert_event_emitted "[SPEC-6] stage.always_run.unresolved is emitted" \
335	    "$ZBUILD_EVENTS_JSONL" "stage.always_run.unresolved"
336	# And it must not change the run's fate — an always-run stage never decides the
337	# verdict, including when it could not be found.
338	assert_eq "[SPEC-6] an unresolvable always-run stage does not fail the run" "0" "$_unres_rc"
339	
340	print_test_results
341

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Integration: #1831 — an `always_run:` stage runs on EVERY exit path.
#
# This is the assertion the attribute exists for. A mechanism that fires on four
# of five exit paths is #1878's defect wearing a new name ("the snapshot was
# never called"), so each path gets its own case and names itself on failure —
# a single parameterised assertion would report "one of five" and leave the
# operator to find which.
#
# Paths covered: rc=0, rc=1, a stage killed by SIGINT (rc=130 + the recorded
# abort word), SIGTERM to the runner, and a release hook that hangs past its
# own timeout_s.
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/../.." && pwd)"
RUNNER="$REPO_ROOT/core/pipeline/runner.sh"

# shellcheck source=../../scripts/lib/helpers.sh
source "$REPO_ROOT/scripts/lib/helpers.sh"
# shellcheck source=../../scripts/lib/test-helpers.sh
source "$REPO_ROOT/scripts/lib/test-helpers.sh"

print_test_header "always_run dispatches on every exit path (#1831)"
setup_test_env "zb-always-run-exit"
export ZBUILD_CONTRACT_VALIDATOR=warn

PLUGINS_ROOT="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/plugins"
export ZBUILD_PLUGINS_ROOT="$PLUGINS_ROOT"
export ZBUILD_EVENTS_DIR="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/events"
export ZBUILD_EVENTS_JSONL="$ZBUILD_EVENTS_DIR/events.jsonl"
export ZBUILD_EVENT_SCHEMA="$REPO_ROOT/config/event-schema.json"
export ZBUILD_MODELS_FILE="$REPO_ROOT/config/models.json"
export ZBUILD_CYCLES_ENABLED=0
export ZBUILD_SCOPE_OVERRIDE=1
mkdir -p "$ZBUILD_EVENTS_DIR" "$HOME/.zbuild"
printf '%s' "bootstrap" > "$HOME/.zbuild/scope-override-token"

OVERLAY_REPO="$(setup_git_temp_repo always-run-overlay)"
install_template_overlay "$OVERLAY_REPO" always-run-minimal

# The always-run plugin, bound by ROLE (not by directory — that coupling is
# what #1831 removes). It touches a marker so "did it run?" is a file test
# rather than an inference from an event that might not be emitted.
mock_plugin_factory "outcome"  "agent" 0 "" ""         >/dev/null
mock_plugin_factory "teardown" "tool"  0 "" "teardown" >/dev/null

RELEASE_MARKER="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/release-ran"
RELEASE_ENTERED="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/release-entered"
_arm_release() {
    # Two markers, not one. ENTERED is written before the optional sleep,
    # RAN after it. With a single completion marker, "the watchdog killed a
    # hanging hook" and "the hook was never dispatched at all" are the same
    # observation — and SPEC-5 passed for that wrong reason during development,
    # before the dispatch worked at all.
    # $1 = optional `sleep N` injected between the two, for the watchdog case.
    cat > "$PLUGINS_ROOT/tool/teardown/plugin.sh" <<PLUG
teardown_run() {
    : > "${RELEASE_ENTERED}"
    ${1:-:}
    : > "${RELEASE_MARKER}"
    return 0
}
PLUG
}

# The stage announces that it is RUNNING (#2029). `pipeline-state.json` appears
# during startup, long before any stage is dispatched, so waiting on it and then
# sleeping a second is not "the stage has started" — it is a guess that happens to
# hold on an idle machine.
#
# On a loaded one it does not, and SPEC-4 then SIGTERMs a runner still setting up
# its worktree: no stage has run, no release hook is armed, no marker is written,
# and the assertion reports a missing file with no hint that the run never got
# that far. Observed directly — `wait` returned in 0s, the hook-entered marker was
# absent, and the runner's last line was "Working in the run's worktree".
#
# `runner-release-exit-paths-test.sh` already does this correctly with
# BUILD_STARTED; this is the same idea. The marker can only appear once the stage
# is genuinely executing, so load can only delay it, never fake it.
# #1850: the stage writes the v2 result its manifest (mock_plugin_factory's)
# promises — pass on rc 0, error/broken otherwise — so a run that should succeed
# is not failed for leaving no readable result.
_arm_outcome() {
    local _o=pass
    [[ "${2:-0}" -ne 0 ]] && _o=broken
    cat > "$PLUGINS_ROOT/agent/outcome/plugin.sh" <<PLUG
outcome_run() {
    : > "\${STAGE_STARTED:-/dev/null}"
    ${1:-:}
    $(mock_result_line outcome "$_o")
    return ${2:-0}
}
PLUG
}

# Each case gets its own state dir: a stale marker or state file from a prior
# case would make a later one pass for the wrong reason.
_run_case() {
    local name="$1" rc_want_set="$2"
    rm -f "$RELEASE_MARKER" "$RELEASE_ENTERED"
    export ZBUILD_STATE_DIR="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/state-$name"
    mkdir -p "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR"
    set +e
    ( cd "$OVERLAY_REPO" && bash "$RUNNER" --template always-run-minimal \
        --goal "always-run $name" ) >"$TEST_TEMP_DIR/$name.out" 2>&1
    _CASE_RC=$?
    set -e
    [[ "$rc_want_set" == "skip" ]] || true
}

# ─── [SPEC-1][change] rc=0 — the ordinary success path ──────────────────────
print_test_section "[SPEC-1][change] release runs when the pipeline succeeds"
_arm_release; _arm_outcome "" 0
_run_case "rc0" skip
assert_file_exists "[SPEC-1] release ran on rc=0" "$RELEASE_MARKER"

# ─── [SPEC-2][change] rc=1 — a failed run still frees its resources ─────────
# The failing path is the one that matters most: a run that died is exactly the
# run holding process groups and locks nobody else will clean up.
print_test_section "[SPEC-2][change] release runs when a stage fails"
_arm_release; _arm_outcome "" 1
_run_case "rc1" skip
assert_file_exists "[SPEC-2] release ran on a non-zero stage rc" "$RELEASE_MARKER"

# ─── [SPEC-3][change] the SIGINT path ─────────────────────────────────────
# #1850 (ADR-054 §4, ADR-025): the SIGINT path is the recorded abort word, not
# rc=130 — a bare 130 from a stage is just a failed stage now. So the stage
# does what a Ctrl-C does to the process group: the sentinel is armed (empty =
# sigint) and the child dies with 130. The run must end on the abort path —
# exit 1, status interrupted — or this case would only repeat SPEC-2.
print_test_section "[SPEC-3][change] release runs on the SIGINT path (abort word sigint)"
_arm_release
# shellcheck disable=SC2016  # expanded by the stage at run time, not here
_arm_outcome ': > "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR/.abort.signal"' 130
_run_case "rc130" skip
assert_file_exists "[SPEC-3] release ran on the SIGINT path" "$RELEASE_MARKER"
assert_eq "[SPEC-3] the run took the abort path: exit 1 (not 130), status interrupted" \
    "1 interrupted" "$_CASE_RC $(jq -r '.status // "MISSING"' "$TEST_TEMP_DIR/state-rc130/pipeline-state.json" 2>/dev/null)"

# ─── [SPEC-4][change] SIGTERM delivered to the runner itself ───────────────
# Distinct from SPEC-3: there the stage returned a code, here the signal is
# delivered to the runner process while a stage is still executing. #1759's
# re-armed INT/TERM traps are what give this path somewhere to hang off.
print_test_section "[SPEC-4][change] release runs when the runner is SIGTERMed mid-stage"
_arm_release; _arm_outcome "sleep 30" 0
rm -f "$RELEASE_MARKER" "$RELEASE_ENTERED"
export ZBUILD_STATE_DIR="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/state-sigterm"
export STAGE_STARTED="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/stage-started-sigterm"
rm -f "$STAGE_STARTED"
mkdir -p "$ZBUILD_STATE_DIR"
( cd "$OVERLAY_REPO" && bash "$RUNNER" --template always-run-minimal \
    --goal "always-run sigterm" ) >"$TEST_TEMP_DIR/sigterm.out" 2>&1 &
_runner_pid=$!
# Wait for the run to actually reach the stage before signalling — signalling a
# runner still in startup would prove nothing about the exit path.
#
# #2029: this used to wait for `pipeline-state.json` and then sleep 1. That file
# is written during STARTUP, so the wait proved nothing and the sleep was the only
# real margin. Under load it was not enough and the signal landed mid-startup.
# STAGE_STARTED is written by the stage itself, so it cannot be reached early.
_waited=0
while [[ ! -f "$STAGE_STARTED" && $_waited -lt 300 ]]; do
    sleep 0.2; _waited=$(( _waited + 1 ))
done
if [[ ! -f "$STAGE_STARTED" ]]; then
    assert_fail "[SPEC-4] the stage started before the signal was sent" \
        "STAGE_STARTED never appeared in 60s — the run never reached a stage, so the exit path was never exercised"
fi
_spec4_t0=$(date +%s)
kill -TERM "$_runner_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
wait "$_runner_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
_spec4_wait_s=$(( $(date +%s) - _spec4_t0 ))
# The trap runs in the dying process; give it a moment to land the marker.
_waited=0
while [[ ! -f "$RELEASE_MARKER" && $_waited -lt 50 ]]; do
    sleep 0.2; _waited=$(( _waited + 1 ))
done

# #2029: say WHAT WAS SEEN, not merely that the file is absent.
#
# This assertion has failed intermittently on CI for as long as it has existed,
# and it could never be diagnosed because "file not found" is the same output
# whether the runner ignored the signal, died before its trap, ran teardown into
# a different path, or simply had not finished yet. Three separate mechanisms
# were proposed for it and all three were disproven.
#

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# core/pipeline/strategies/sequential.sh — serialized per-platform dispatch (issue #200/#222)
# ADR-009: platforms run one at a time; always halts on the first collect failure.
# Depends on core/orch/contract.sh being sourced first by the caller (runner.sh).
# Sourced library: inherits caller's pipefail; do not add set -euo pipefail here.

[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_STRATEGY_SEQUENTIAL_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
_ZBUILD_STRATEGY_SEQUENTIAL_LOADED=1

_ZBUILD_STRATEGIES_DIR_SEQ="$(cd "${BASH_SOURCE[0]%/*}" 2>/dev/null || true; pwd)"
source "${_ZBUILD_STRATEGIES_DIR_SEQ}/common.sh"

# ─── _strategy_run_sequential ────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Usage: _strategy_run_sequential <pool_id> <stage> <roles_out> <state_file> <plugins_root>
#   pool_id    — caller-supplied, already validated
#   stage      — stage name
#   roles_out  — newline-delimited list of role names
#   state_file — path to pipeline state file
#   plugins_root — path to plugins directory
#
# Dispatches one work unit at a time via orch_dispatch + orch_collect.
# Halts on first failure (does not continue to next platform/role).
# Always calls orch_shutdown on exit (success or failure).
# Artifact enforcement happens per work unit inside plugin_hook_call (#1906).
#
# Returns:
#   0 — all succeeded
#   1 — any collect/dispatch failure
#   4 — no plugin found for any role (caller may fall back to stage-id lookup)
_strategy_run_sequential() {
    # #1850 (ADR-054 §4): rc is 0 or 1; WHY rides this word, which the caller
    # reads in the same shell — ok | partial | empty | no_plugin | bad_dimension
    # | infra_failed | failed.
    _ZB_STRATEGY_OUTCOME="failed"
    local pool_id="$1" stage="$2" roles_out="$3" state_file="$4" plugins_root="$5"
    local any_plugin_found=false

    local role platform plugin_dir wu prc
    while IFS= read -r role; do
        [[ -z "$role" ]] && continue
        for platform in "${_DETECTED_PLATFORMS[@]}"; do
            plugin_dir="$(resolve_plugin_for_role "$role" "$platform" "$plugins_root" 2>/dev/null || true)"
            [[ -z "$plugin_dir" ]] && \
                plugin_dir="$(resolve_plugin_for_role "$role" "" "$plugins_root" 2>/dev/null || true)"
            [[ -z "$plugin_dir" ]] && continue
            any_plugin_found=true

            wu="$(_strategy_make_work_unit "$plugin_dir" "$stage" "$state_file" "$platform")" || {
                warn "sequential: failed to create work unit for role=$role platform=$platform" || true
                orch_shutdown "$pool_id" 2>/dev/null || true
                return 1
            }

            orch_dispatch "$pool_id" "$wu" >/dev/null || {
                warn "sequential: orch_dispatch failed for role=$role platform=$platform" || true
                rm -f "$wu" 2>/dev/null || true
                orch_shutdown "$pool_id" 2>/dev/null || true
                return 1
            }

            prc=0
            orch_collect "$pool_id" --timeout "$(template_stage_time_limit "$stage")" || prc=$?
            rm -f "$wu" 2>/dev/null || true

            if [[ $prc -ne 0 ]]; then
                if [[ "${_ORCH_COLLECT_OUTCOME:-}" == "timed_out" ]]; then
                    local _seq_limit; _seq_limit="$(template_stage_time_limit "$stage")"
                    warn "sequential: stage '${stage}' timed out after ${_seq_limit}s" || true
                    orch_shutdown "$pool_id" 2>/dev/null || true
                    _ZB_STRATEGY_OUTCOME="timed_out"
                else
                    warn "sequential: stage=$stage role=$role platform=$platform failed (rc=$prc)" || true
                    orch_shutdown "$pool_id" 2>/dev/null || true
                fi
                return 1
            fi

        done
    done <<< "$roles_out"

    orch_shutdown "$pool_id" 2>/dev/null || true
    $any_plugin_found || { _ZB_STRATEGY_OUTCOME="no_plugin"; return 1; }
    _ZB_STRATEGY_OUTCOME="ok"
    return 0
}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Guard: the orch-sequential plugin is removed from the installed tree (#1801,
# SPEC-3). A guard that passes while the directory still exists would let a
# trivially-present plugin defeat the whole point of SPEC-2's no-fallback rule.
#
# Two assertions:
#   1. The plugin directory itself does not exist in the installed tree.
#   2. No code or config file outside docs/adr/ still names "orch-sequential"
#      (the golden file, manifests, contract.sh hardcoded path, test references).
#
# Both must FAIL on current code (the directory exists and is referenced
# throughout) and PASS after the implementation removes the plugin.
#
# [#1801/SPEC-3]
set -uo pipefail

REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)"
source "$REPO_ROOT/scripts/lib/test-helpers.sh"

print_test_header "orch-sequential is absent from the installed tree (#1801 SPEC-3)"
setup_test_env "orch-sequential-absent-guard"

# ── SPEC-3a: plugin directory does not exist ─────────────────────────────────
_orch_seq_dir="$REPO_ROOT/plugins/tool/orch-sequential"
if [[ ! -d "$_orch_seq_dir" ]]; then
    assert_pass "[#1801/SPEC-3] orch-sequential plugin directory does not exist"
else
    assert_fail "[#1801/SPEC-3] orch-sequential plugin directory does not exist" \
        "directory still present: $_orch_seq_dir"
fi

# ── SPEC-3b: no code or config file outside docs/adr/ names orch-sequential ──
# Files allowed to reference orch-sequential: docs/adr/ (ADR prose)
# Files NOT allowed: core/, plugins/, scripts/, config/, tests/, .github/
_hits=""
while IFS= read -r _f; do
    # Skip docs/adr/ — ADR prose is allowed to name the deleted plugin
    case "$_f" in
        */docs/adr/*) continue ;;
        # Skip the guard test itself (this file)
        */orch-sequential-absent-guard-test.sh) continue ;;
    esac
    _hits="${_hits}${_f}"$'\n'
done < <(grep -rl "orch-sequential" \
    "$REPO_ROOT/core" \
    "$REPO_ROOT/plugins" \
    "$REPO_ROOT/scripts" \
    "$REPO_ROOT/config" \
    "$REPO_ROOT/tests" \
    "$REPO_ROOT/.github" \
    2>/dev/null || true)

# Remove trailing newline for display
_hits="${_hits%$'\n'}"
if [[ -z "$_hits" ]]; then
    assert_pass "[#1801/SPEC-3] no code or config file outside docs/adr/ names orch-sequential"
else
    assert_fail "[#1801/SPEC-3] no code or config file outside docs/adr/ names orch-sequential" \
        "still referenced in: $(printf '%s' "$_hits" | tr '\n' ' ')"
fi

# ── SPEC-3c: golden file does not exist ─────────────────────────────────────
# Directly assert the golden file is absent — a file by that name whose
# content lacks the string 'orch-sequential' would pass the grep above but
# still violate the requirement.
_golden_file="$REPO_ROOT/tests/golden/orch-sequential-capabilities.golden"
if [[ ! -f "$_golden_file" ]]; then
    assert_pass "[#1801/SPEC-3] tests/golden/orch-sequential-capabilities.golden does not exist"
else
    assert_fail "[#1801/SPEC-3] tests/golden/orch-sequential-capabilities.golden must not exist" \
        "file still present: $_golden_file"
fi

print_test_results

id: always-run-minimal
name: Always-Run Minimal Pipeline
extends: simple
defaults:
  strategy: fanout

# #1831 fixture: the smallest template that exercises `always_run:`.
#
# NEW shape (`flow:` + top-level sections) on purpose — but NOT because
# `always_run:` needs it. The key is shape-INDEPENDENT: `_tpl_parse_always_run`
# reads it straight from the file, and SPEC-6 in tests/unit/template-always-run-test.sh
# proves an old-shape template inherits it too. The new shape is used here only
# because it is the smaller fixture, and because it exercises the per-repo
# overlay's new-shape path alongside it.
#
# `outcome` is the only flow stage. Its plugin is replaced per-case by the test
# so one fixture can drive every exit path: rc=0, rc=1, SIGINT (rc=130), SIGTERM
# and a hang past the timeout. `release` is never in the flow — the whole point
# is that it runs anyway.
flow:
  - outcome

always_run:
  - release

outcome:
  gate: auto
  io:
    destinations: [file]
    tail_lines: 50

# timeout_s is deliberately small so the watchdog case does not stretch the
# suite's wall clock. The bound itself is what SPEC-5 asserts.
release:
  gate: auto
  roles: [teardown]
  router:
    timeout_s: 2
  io:
    destinations: [file]
    tail_lines: 50

Let me check what `template_stage_time_limit` does:

content.content:
1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# scripts/lib/stage-time-limit.sh — the whole-stage time limit (ADR-063, amended
3	# 2026-10-15). Read from the loaded template (_TPL_SOURCE_FILE, exported by
4	# load_template), so every dispatch arm — the map arm's generated script
5	# included — sees the same value.
6	#
7	# Sourced library: inherits the caller's shell options; do NOT add set -euo.
8	
9	[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_STAGE_TIME_LIMIT_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
10	_ZBUILD_STAGE_TIME_LIMIT_LOADED=1
11	
12	# Per-stage `timeout_s:` — how long the engine lets the WHOLE stage run before
13	# it stops it (every model call, check and retry inside it). Not router.timeout_s,
14	# which bounds one model call. 900 seconds (15 minutes) when unset. Read lazily
15	# from the template source, like template_stage_retry.
16	template_stage_time_limit() {
17	    local _tstl; template_stage_time_limit_v _tstl "$1"; printf '%s' "$_tstl"
18	}
19	# template_stage_time_limit_v <var> <stage> — the same into <var>. One read of
20	# the template gives every stage's limit (template_stage_time_limits_load), and
21	# load_template makes that read in the runner's shell, so every dispatch
22	# inherits it (ADR-065 §5): asked per stage, the read was redone in each
23	# dispatch's subshell.
24	declare -gA _ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO=()   # "<template>\034<stage>" → its timeout_s text; "<template>\034" → read
25	template_stage_time_limit_v() {
26	    local -n _tstv="$1"
27	    template_stage_time_limits_load
28	    _tstv="${_ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO["${_TPL_SOURCE_FILE:-}"$'\034'"$2"]:-}"
29	    [[ "$_tstv" =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || _tstv=900
30	}
31	
32	# template_stage_time_limits_load — every stage's `timeout_s:` from the template,
33	# in one pass, into _ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO; once per template (…_reload reads again).
34	# A stage's limit is its block's own `timeout_s:` one level in: the block opens
35	# at `<stage>:` in column 0, or two deep under `stage_definitions:`, and closes
36	# at the next line no deeper than its header; the first such line wins, and a
37	# block can open again further down. Every stage is followed at once, rule for
38	# rule as the per-stage reader this replaces (tests/unit/shell-work-cost-test.sh
39	# W5 holds the two equal).

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/lib/stage-time-limit.sh — the whole-stage time limit (ADR-063, amended
# 2026-10-15). Read from the loaded template (_TPL_SOURCE_FILE, exported by
# load_template), so every dispatch arm — the map arm's generated script
# included — sees the same value.
#
# Sourced library: inherits the caller's shell options; do NOT add set -euo.

[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_STAGE_TIME_LIMIT_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
_ZBUILD_STAGE_TIME_LIMIT_LOADED=1

# Per-stage `timeout_s:` — how long the engine lets the WHOLE stage run before
# it stops it (every model call, check and retry inside it). Not router.timeout_s,
# which bounds one model call. 900 seconds (15 minutes) when unset. Read lazily
# from the template source, like template_stage_retry.
template_stage_time_limit() {
    local _tstl; template_stage_time_limit_v _tstl "$1"; printf '%s' "$_tstl"
}
# template_stage_time_limit_v <var> <stage> — the same into <var>. One read of
# the template gives every stage's limit (template_stage_time_limits_load), and
# load_template makes that read in the runner's shell, so every dispatch
# inherits it (ADR-065 §5): asked per stage, the read was redone in each
# dispatch's subshell.
declare -gA _ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO=()   # "<template>\034<stage>" → its timeout_s text; "<template>\034" → read
template_stage_time_limit_v() {
    local -n _tstv="$1"
    template_stage_time_limits_load
    _tstv="${_ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO["${_TPL_SOURCE_FILE:-}"$'\034'"$2"]:-}"
    [[ "$_tstv" =~ ^[1-9][0-9]*$ ]] || _tstv=900
}

# template_stage_time_limits_load — every stage's `timeout_s:` from the template,
# in one pass, into _ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO; once per template (…_reload reads again).
# A stage's limit is its block's own `timeout_s:` one level in: the block opens
# at `<stage>:` in column 0, or two deep under `stage_definitions:`, and closes
# at the next line no deeper than its header; the first such line wins, and a
# block can open again further down. Every stage is followed at once, rule for
# rule as the per-stage reader this replaces (tests/unit/shell-work-cost-test.sh
# W5 holds the two equal).
template_stage_time_limits_load() {
    local f="${_TPL_SOURCE_FILE:-}"
    [[ -n "$f" ]] || return 0
    [[ -n "${_ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO["$f"$'\034']+x}" ]] && return 0
    _ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO["$f"$'\034']=1
    [[ -f "$f" ]] || return 0
    local line lead li in_defs=0 s s1 s4 s4_was v
    local -A open=() ind=() found=()
    while IFS= read -r line || [[ -n "$line" ]]; do
        if [[ "$line" =~ ^stage_definitions:[[:space:]]*$ ]]; then in_defs=1; continue; fi
        lead="${line%%[! ]*}"; li=${#lead}
        s1=""; [[ "$line" =~ ^([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*):[[:space:]]*$ ]] && s1="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        (( in_defs )) && [[ "$line" =~ ^[a-zA-Z_] ]] && in_defs=0
        s4=""; (( in_defs )) && [[ "$line" =~ ^\ \ ([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*):[[:space:]]*$ ]] && s4="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"
        s4_was="${s4:+${open[$s4]:-}}"
        for s in "${!open[@]}"; do
            if [[ "$line" =~ [^[:space:]] ]] && (( li <= ind[$s] )); then unset 'open[$s]'; continue; fi
            if (( li == ind[$s] + 2 )) && [[ "$line" =~ ^[[:space:]]+timeout_s:[[:space:]]* ]]; then
                v="${line:${#BASH_REMATCH[0]}}"
                if [[ "$v" == *#* ]]; then v="${v%%#*}"; v="${v%"${v##*[![:space:]]}"}"; fi
                _ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO["$f"$'\034'"$s"]="${v//[[:space:]]/}"
                found[$s]=1; unset 'open[$s]'
            fi
        done
        if [[ -n "$s1" && -z "${found[$s1]:-}" ]]; then open[$s1]=1; ind[$s1]=0; fi
        if [[ -n "$s4" && -z "${found[$s4]:-}" && -z "$s4_was" ]]; then open[$s4]=1; ind[$s4]=2; fi
    done 2>/dev/null < "$f"
}

# template_stage_time_limits_reload — forget the template's limits and read it
# again: load_template's call, as the file may have changed since it was read.
template_stage_time_limits_reload() {
    local f="${_TPL_SOURCE_FILE:-}" k
    [[ -n "$f" ]] || return 0
    for k in "${!_ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO[@]}"; do
        [[ "$k" == "$f"$'\034'* ]] && unset "_ZB_STAGE_TL_MEMO[$k]"
    done
    template_stage_time_limits_load
}

The `template_stage_time_limits_load` function reads `timeout_s:` when it's one level in from the stage block header. The key line is:
```bash
if (( li == ind[$s] + 2 )) && [[ "$line" =~ ^[[:space:]]+timeout_s:[[:space:]]* ]]; then
```

For a stage like:
```yaml
release:
  gate: auto
  roles: [teardown]
  router:
    timeout_s: 2
```

The `release:` block opens with `ind[release]=0`, and `timeout_s:` lines at `li=2` (2 spaces indent) would be parsed. But `router.timeout_s` is at `li=4`, which doesn't match.
For simple.yaml, the top-level `timeout_s: 30` sits at li=2 which matches the offset and gets read as 30. But for `always-run-minimal.yaml`, the release stage has no top-level timeout_s field at that depth, only the nested one under `router:` at li=4, so the function would fail to find a match there.

This is the actual bug: `always-run-minimal.yaml` sets `router.timeout_s: 2` but lacks a top-level `release.timeout_s`, so `template_stage_time_limit("release")` falls back to the 900-second default instead of 2. The fix is to add `timeout_s: 2` at the top level of the release block, but I need to check whether this file is even within my scope.

So the real problem is the 2s timeout isn't actually wired to the template value, since that file is out of scope for me to edit. I should check whether `runner-release-exit-paths-test.sh`, which is in scope, is actually the same test or a separate one that I need to focus on instead.

install_template_overlay "$OVERLAY_REPO" resume-minimal
export ZBUILD_SCOPE_OVERRIDE=1
mkdir -p "$HOME/.zbuild"
printf '%s' "bootstrap" > "$HOME/.zbuild/scope-override-token"

_case_no=0
# _prep <name> — fresh state dir + marker for one exit path.
_prep() {
    _case_no=$((_case_no + 1))
    CASE_DIR="$TEST_TEMP_DIR/case-$_case_no-$1"
    mkdir -p "$CASE_DIR/state" "$CASE_DIR/events"
    export ZBUILD_STATE_DIR="$CASE_DIR/state"
    export ZBUILD_EVENTS_DIR="$CASE_DIR/events"
    export ZBUILD_EVENTS_JSONL="$CASE_DIR/events/events.jsonl"
    export RELEASE_MARKER="$CASE_DIR/release-marker"
    export BUILD_STARTED="$CASE_DIR/build-started"
    : > "$RELEASE_MARKER"
    unset BUILD_RC BUILD_SLEEP BUILD_ARM_ABORT 2>/dev/null || true
}

# _assert_released <case> <stage>... — EVERY named stage released, purge never.
#
# #1989: this used to grep the shared marker for any ':release' and pass. Three
# stages append to that one file, so one stage releasing masked two that never
# did — measured: neutering build_cleanup alone left the suite green, and it
# took neutering all three to turn it red. The assertion could only ever detect
# a TOTAL failure of the mechanism, never a partial one, which is the shape a
# real regression takes (#1748: suites observed alive 15+ min after exit).
#
# Each case now names the stages whose cleanup must have run. The sets differ
# by exit path because a stage only reaches release once it has been dispatched.
#
# ADR-062 §2: reclamation reads the process group recorded at DISPATCH, not the
# completion status map, so a stage killed mid-flight IS reclaimable. SPEC-4 and
# SPEC-5 therefore expect `build` as well as `intake` — build had demonstrably
# started (it wrote BUILD_STARTED) before the signal landed. Before #2001 both
# freed `intake` only, because teardown iterated `.stage_statuses`, which
# `_update_stage_status` writes only on complete/failed — i.e. after a stage
# returns, which a killed stage never does.
_assert_released() {
    local _case="$1"; shift
    local _marker; _marker="$(cat "$RELEASE_MARKER" 2>/dev/null || true)"
    local _stage _missing=""
    for _stage in "$@"; do
        grep -q "^${_stage}:release$" <<< "$_marker" || _missing="${_missing}${_stage} "
    done
    if [[ -z "$_missing" ]]; then
        assert_pass "[$_case] cleanup dispatched with scope=release for: $*"
    else
        assert_fail "[$_case] cleanup dispatched with scope=release for: $*" \
            "no release from: ${_missing}| marker=$(tr '\n' ' ' <<< "$_marker")"
    fi
    if grep -q ':purge' <<< "$_marker"; then
        assert_fail "[$_case] purge is never reachable from a run" "marker contained purge"
    else
        assert_pass "[$_case] purge is never reachable from a run"
    fi
}

# SPEC-6 and SPEC-6b each wait out the release bound on purpose: their hook
# blocks, and the bound (the base template's release `timeout_s:` at the
# top-level stage block, 30s after #1801) is what ends it. Started here, each
# from its own repo, so that bound runs while SPEC-1..5 do; their assertions
# are made below, in order.
#
# SPEC-5 (#1801): a separate blocking run uses a template with timeout_s: 5
# for release (NOT router.timeout_s: 5) — old code reads router.timeout_s: 30
# and takes ~30s; new code reads template_stage_time_limit (timeout_s: 5) and
# exits in ~5s. Started here so it runs in parallel with SPEC-6/6b.
_start_blocking() {   # <case name> <hook switch> [template-id]
    local _repo; _repo="$(setup_git_temp_repo "release-exit-paths-$1")"
    install_template_overlay "$_repo" resume-minimal
    local _tpl="${3:-resume-minimal}"
    (
        _prep "$1"

-    local sequential_sh="${_ZBUILD_ROOT}/plugins/tool/orch-sequential/plugin.sh"
-    if [[ "$backend" == "sequential" && -f "$sequential_sh" ]]; then
-        # shellcheck disable=SC1090
-        source "$sequential_sh"

-        return 0
-    fi
-

-    if [[ -f "$sequential_sh" ]]; then
-        warn "orch_load_backend: backend '${backend}' not found; falling back to sequential" || true
-        # shellcheck disable=SC1090

-        _ZBUILD_ORCH_BACKEND_LOADED=1

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# scripts/lib/proc-group.sh — process-group resolution and kill helpers.
3	# Extracted from core/router/route.sh (Wave 15-G, #687) so the test stage and
4	# any other long-running spawn share one implementation (#1748).
5	# Sourced library: no set -euo pipefail.
6	
7	[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_PROC_GROUP_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
8	_ZBUILD_PROC_GROUP_LOADED=1
9	
10	# #2056: there is no setsid prefix any more. Process groups come from `set -m`
11	# at the spawn site — bash job control makes a backgrounded job a group leader,
12	# which is POSIX and identical on macOS and Linux.
13	#
14	# `setsid -w` was wrong here twice over. It is absent on macOS (util-linux is
15	# keg-only), so the prefix went empty, no group was created, and an abort
16	# degraded to a single-PID kill while every descendant survived — the Wave 15-G
17	# guarantee held on Linux only, and the test covering it is Linux-only too, so
18	# nothing said so. And `-w` forces setsid to fork, because it waits for the
19	# child and returns its exit status, so the pid the caller captured was the
20	# wrapper rather than the new session leader.
21	#
22	# Do not reintroduce a prefix here. A spawn that needs an external binary to get
23	# a process group is a spawn whose guarantee is platform-conditional.
24	
25	# Prints the PGID safe to signal for <pid>, or nothing. Empty is not "no group":
26	# it means the group could not be proven distinct from ours, and signalling it
27	# would take down the runner itself — so callers must fall back to a PID kill.
28	zbuild_pg_resolve() {
29	    local _pid="${1:-}"
30	    [[ -n "$_pid" && "$_pid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
31	    local _child _self
32	    _child="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$_pid" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
33	    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
34	    if [[ -n "$_child" && -n "$_self" && "$_child" != "$_self" ]]; then
35	        printf '%s' "$_child"
36	        return 0
37	    fi
38	    # A short-lived child can exit before `ps` reports it. Under `set -m` the
39	    # spawn IS the group leader, so PGID == PID by construction and that stays
40	    # true after it is gone — reporting the pid is correct, not a guess.
41	    #
42	    # This branch previously justified itself with "setsid execs in place, so it
43	    # needs no fork". That was false under `-w` (#2056): setsid forks in order to
44	    # wait, so the captured pid was the wrapper and the group belonged to a
45	    # process one fork below. Under job control there is no wrapper to be wrong
46	    # about.
47	    if [[ -z "$_child" ]]; then
48	        printf '%s' "$_pid"
49	    fi
50	}
51	
52	# TERM <target>, then KILL whatever is left after <grace_s>. Shared by the group
53	# and single-PID paths so both get the same grace — the escalation is the whole
54	# contract, and a caller that skips it is indistinguishable from a plain KILL.
55	#
56	# Synchronous by construction (#905): the `{ sleep 1 && kill -KILL; } &` backstop
57	# this replaces could outlive the caller that armed it, so teardown returned
58	# while the tree was still alive and the backstop was sometimes lost with it.
59	# Polling instead costs milliseconds when the target exits on TERM, costs the
60	# full grace only when it ignores TERM, and leaves nothing running on return.
61	_zbuild_pg_term_then_kill() {
62	    # `--` because a group target is spelled `-PGID` and would otherwise parse
63	    # as an option.
64	    local _target="$1" _grace="$2"
65	    kill -TERM -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || true
66	    local _ticks=$(( _grace * 10 )) _i=0
67	    while (( _i < _ticks )); do
68	        kill -0 -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || return 0
69	        sleep 0.1 2>/dev/null || true
70	        _i=$(( _i + 1 ))
71	    done
72	    kill -KILL -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || true
73	}
74	
75	# A non-numeric grace would evaluate to 0 in the arithmetic context above, so the
76	# poll loop would never run and the target would go straight to KILL — silently
77	# losing the escalation the caller asked for. Clamp to the default instead.
78	_zbuild_pg_grace() {
79	    local _g="${1:-1}"
80	    [[ "$_g" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && "$_g" -gt 0 ]] && printf '%s' "$_g" || printf '1'
81	}
82	
83	# zbuild_pg_record_pgid <file> — the pgid out of a `.pgid` record.
84	#
85	# ONE reader, because there are two formats on disk and three places that read
86	# them (#2018). The engine's dispatch record is `<pgid>\t<leader start time>`;
87	# tool/test's own `test-stage.pgid` is a bare number; and a record written before
88	# #2018 is bare too. A reader that only understands one of those does not error —
89	# it fails the numeric guard and `continue`s, so the caller kills NOTHING and
90	# reports success. That is how a format change here silently disables ADR-062 §2
91	# reclamation, which is the path that actually runs on every normal exit.
92	#
93	# Prints nothing and returns 1 when there is no usable pgid, so a caller can
94	# still distinguish "no record" from "record says 1234".
95	zbuild_pg_record_pgid() {
96	    local _f="${1:-}" _pgid=""
97	    [[ -n "$_f" && -f "$_f" ]] || return 1
98	    IFS=$'\t' read -r _pgid _ 2>/dev/null < "$_f" || true
99	    [[ "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 1
100	    printf '%s' "$_pgid"
101	}
102	
103	# zbuild_pg_register <pgid> — record a process group the caller just created.
104	#
105	# ADR-062 §1 had the ENGINE record this at dispatch. It could not, and the reason
106	# is structural: a stage is a bash function call, not a subprocess, so at the
107	# dispatch seam no group exists yet. That code fell back to `$$`'s group — the
108	# engine's own — which teardown then skipped, correctly, because signalling your
109	# own group takes the runner down with it. Every record was unkillable, every
110	# record was skipped, and §2's kill loop never freed anything (#2024).
111	#
112	# So the direction reverses: whoever CREATES a group registers it. Two sites do,
113	# and only two — `tool/test`'s `set -m` suite and the router's `setsid` spawn.
114	#
115	# Refusing to register our own group is the invariant, not a safety check. A
116	# record naming the registrar's own group is strictly worse than no record: it
117	# cannot be acted on, and it makes the mechanism look live while it does nothing
118	# — which is exactly how the original defect survived #2001, #2018 and an ADR.
119	#
120	# Fail-open throughout: a spawn is never refused because bookkeeping was
121	# unavailable. Silence here costs a possible leak; failing here costs the run.
122	zbuild_pg_register() {
123	    local _pgid="${1:-}"
124	    [[ -n "$_pgid" && "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
125	    local _self
126	    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
127	    [[ -n "$_self" && "$_self" == "$_pgid" ]] && return 0
128	    local _sd="${ZBUILD_STATE_DIR:-}"
129	    [[ -n "$_sd" && -d "$_sd" ]] || return 0
130	    local _stage="${2:-${ZBUILD_CURRENT_STAGE:-}}"
131	    [[ -n "$_stage" ]] || return 0
132	    # One path component, sanitised the same way stage scratch keys are, so no
133	    # stage name can climb out of runtime/.
134	    _stage="${_stage//[^A-Za-z0-9_-]/_}"
135	    local _dir="${_sd}/runtime/stages"
136	    mkdir -p "$_dir" 2>/dev/null || return 0
137	    # #2018 format: the leader's start time proves the pgid still names what
138	    # recorded it, so a later sweep cannot signal a recycled pid.
139	    local _start
140	    _start="$(ps -o lstart= -p "$_pgid" 2>/dev/null | tr -s ' ' | sed 's/^ *//;s/ *$//' || true)"
141	    printf '%s\t%s' "$_pgid" "$_start" > "${_dir}/${_stage}.pgid" 2>/dev/null || true
142	    return 0
143	}
144	
145	# TERM then KILL a whole process group. `-PGID` is the negative-pid convention.
146	zbuild_pg_kill() {
147	    local _pgid="${1:-}"
148	    [[ -n "$_pgid" && "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
149	    # Refuse our own group: `kill -- -PGID` from inside it takes down the runner.
150	    local _self
151	    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
152	    [[ -n "$_self" && "$_self" == "$_pgid" ]] && return 0
153	    _zbuild_pg_term_then_kill "-$_pgid" "$(_zbuild_pg_grace "${2:-}")"
154	}
155	
156	# TERM then KILL a single PID — the path taken when no group could be proven.
157	# It gets the same grace as the group path: a suite that flushes coverage or
158	# writes partial results on SIGTERM needs the window wherever it is killed from.
159	zbuild_pid_kill() {
160	    local _pid="${1:-}"
161	    [[ -n "$_pid" && "$_pid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
162	    _zbuild_pg_term_then_kill "$_pid" "$(_zbuild_pg_grace "${2:-}")"
163	}

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/lib/proc-group.sh — process-group resolution and kill helpers.
# Extracted from core/router/route.sh (Wave 15-G, #687) so the test stage and
# any other long-running spawn share one implementation (#1748).
# Sourced library: no set -euo pipefail.

[[ -n "${_ZBUILD_PROC_GROUP_LOADED:-}" ]] && return 0
_ZBUILD_PROC_GROUP_LOADED=1

# #2056: there is no setsid prefix any more. Process groups come from `set -m`
# at the spawn site — bash job control makes a backgrounded job a group leader,
# which is POSIX and identical on macOS and Linux.
#
# `setsid -w` was wrong here twice over. It is absent on macOS (util-linux is
# keg-only), so the prefix went empty, no group was created, and an abort
# degraded to a single-PID kill while every descendant survived — the Wave 15-G
# guarantee held on Linux only, and the test covering it is Linux-only too, so
# nothing said so. And `-w` forces setsid to fork, because it waits for the
# child and returns its exit status, so the pid the caller captured was the
# wrapper rather than the new session leader.
#
# Do not reintroduce a prefix here. A spawn that needs an external binary to get
# a process group is a spawn whose guarantee is platform-conditional.

# Prints the PGID safe to signal for <pid>, or nothing. Empty is not "no group":
# it means the group could not be proven distinct from ours, and signalling it
# would take down the runner itself — so callers must fall back to a PID kill.
zbuild_pg_resolve() {
    local _pid="${1:-}"
    [[ -n "$_pid" && "$_pid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
    local _child _self
    _child="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$_pid" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
    if [[ -n "$_child" && -n "$_self" && "$_child" != "$_self" ]]; then
        printf '%s' "$_child"
        return 0
    fi
    # A short-lived child can exit before `ps` reports it. Under `set -m` the
    # spawn IS the group leader, so PGID == PID by construction and that stays
    # true after it is gone — reporting the pid is correct, not a guess.
    #
    # This branch previously justified itself with "setsid execs in place, so it
    # needs no fork". That was false under `-w` (#2056): setsid forks in order to
    # wait, so the captured pid was the wrapper and the group belonged to a
    # process one fork below. Under job control there is no wrapper to be wrong
    # about.
    if [[ -z "$_child" ]]; then
        printf '%s' "$_pid"
    fi
}

# TERM <target>, then KILL whatever is left after <grace_s>. Shared by the group
# and single-PID paths so both get the same grace — the escalation is the whole
# contract, and a caller that skips it is indistinguishable from a plain KILL.
#
# Synchronous by construction (#905): the `{ sleep 1 && kill -KILL; } &` backstop
# this replaces could outlive the caller that armed it, so teardown returned
# while the tree was still alive and the backstop was sometimes lost with it.
# Polling instead costs milliseconds when the target exits on TERM, costs the
# full grace only when it ignores TERM, and leaves nothing running on return.
_zbuild_pg_term_then_kill() {
    # `--` because a group target is spelled `-PGID` and would otherwise parse
    # as an option.
    local _target="$1" _grace="$2"
    kill -TERM -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || true
    local _ticks=$(( _grace * 10 )) _i=0
    while (( _i < _ticks )); do
        kill -0 -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || return 0
        sleep 0.1 2>/dev/null || true
        _i=$(( _i + 1 ))
    done
    kill -KILL -- "$_target" 2>/dev/null || true
}

# A non-numeric grace would evaluate to 0 in the arithmetic context above, so the
# poll loop would never run and the target would go straight to KILL — silently
# losing the escalation the caller asked for. Clamp to the default instead.
_zbuild_pg_grace() {
    local _g="${1:-1}"
    [[ "$_g" =~ ^[0-9]+$ && "$_g" -gt 0 ]] && printf '%s' "$_g" || printf '1'
}

# zbuild_pg_record_pgid <file> — the pgid out of a `.pgid` record.
#
# ONE reader, because there are two formats on disk and three places that read
# them (#2018). The engine's dispatch record is `<pgid>\t<leader start time>`;
# tool/test's own `test-stage.pgid` is a bare number; and a record written before
# #2018 is bare too. A reader that only understands one of those does not error —
# it fails the numeric guard and `continue`s, so the caller kills NOTHING and
# reports success. That is how a format change here silently disables ADR-062 §2
# reclamation, which is the path that actually runs on every normal exit.
#
# Prints nothing and returns 1 when there is no usable pgid, so a caller can
# still distinguish "no record" from "record says 1234".
zbuild_pg_record_pgid() {
    local _f="${1:-}" _pgid=""
    [[ -n "$_f" && -f "$_f" ]] || return 1
    IFS=$'\t' read -r _pgid _ 2>/dev/null < "$_f" || true
    [[ "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 1
    printf '%s' "$_pgid"
}

# zbuild_pg_register <pgid> — record a process group the caller just created.
#
# ADR-062 §1 had the ENGINE record this at dispatch. It could not, and the reason
# is structural: a stage is a bash function call, not a subprocess, so at the
# dispatch seam no group exists yet. That code fell back to `$$`'s group — the
# engine's own — which teardown then skipped, correctly, because signalling your
# own group takes the runner down with it. Every record was unkillable, every
# record was skipped, and §2's kill loop never freed anything (#2024).
#
# So the direction reverses: whoever CREATES a group registers it. Two sites do,
# and only two — `tool/test`'s `set -m` suite and the router's `setsid` spawn.
#
# Refusing to register our own group is the invariant, not a safety check. A
# record naming the registrar's own group is strictly worse than no record: it
# cannot be acted on, and it makes the mechanism look live while it does nothing
# — which is exactly how the original defect survived #2001, #2018 and an ADR.
#
# Fail-open throughout: a spawn is never refused because bookkeeping was
# unavailable. Silence here costs a possible leak; failing here costs the run.
zbuild_pg_register() {
    local _pgid="${1:-}"
    [[ -n "$_pgid" && "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
    local _self
    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
    [[ -n "$_self" && "$_self" == "$_pgid" ]] && return 0
    local _sd="${ZBUILD_STATE_DIR:-}"
    [[ -n "$_sd" && -d "$_sd" ]] || return 0
    local _stage="${2:-${ZBUILD_CURRENT_STAGE:-}}"
    [[ -n "$_stage" ]] || return 0
    # One path component, sanitised the same way stage scratch keys are, so no
    # stage name can climb out of runtime/.
    _stage="${_stage//[^A-Za-z0-9_-]/_}"
    local _dir="${_sd}/runtime/stages"
    mkdir -p "$_dir" 2>/dev/null || return 0
    # #2018 format: the leader's start time proves the pgid still names what
    # recorded it, so a later sweep cannot signal a recycled pid.
    local _start
    _start="$(ps -o lstart= -p "$_pgid" 2>/dev/null | tr -s ' ' | sed 's/^ *//;s/ *$//' || true)"
    printf '%s\t%s' "$_pgid" "$_start" > "${_dir}/${_stage}.pgid" 2>/dev/null || true
    return 0
}

# TERM then KILL a whole process group. `-PGID` is the negative-pid convention.
zbuild_pg_kill() {
    local _pgid="${1:-}"
    [[ -n "$_pgid" && "$_pgid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
    # Refuse our own group: `kill -- -PGID` from inside it takes down the runner.
    local _self
    _self="$(ps -o pgid= -p "$$" 2>/dev/null | tr -d ' ' || true)"
    [[ -n "$_self" && "$_self" == "$_pgid" ]] && return 0
    _zbuild_pg_term_then_kill "-$_pgid" "$(_zbuild_pg_grace "${2:-}")"
}

# TERM then KILL a single PID — the path taken when no group could be proven.
# It gets the same grace as the group path: a suite that flushes coverage or
# writes partial results on SIGTERM needs the window wherever it is killed from.
zbuild_pid_kill() {
    local _pid="${1:-}"
    [[ -n "$_pid" && "$_pid" =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || return 0
    _zbuild_pg_term_then_kill "$_pid" "$(_zbuild_pg_grace "${2:-}")"
}
